newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to send hijacker back to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China says to send hijacker back to Taiwan.

text.p: China on Thursday gave in to Taiwan's demands to repatriate a man who forced a Taiwanese airliner to the mainland this month, but demanded the island send back 16 Chinese hijackers in return.
"Liu Shan-chung ... will be repatriated to Taiwan after necessary investigations are made," the Xinhua news agency said, quoting the semi-official Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits.
It did not give a date for the repatriation of Liu, who hijacked a domestic Taiwanese airliner on March 10 and forced it to China's southeastern city of Xiamen.

The association handles bilateral ties in the absence of formal links between Beijing and Taipei, rivals since the communists won the Chinese civil war and drove the defeated Nationalists into exile on Taiwan in 1949.
The association official said China was repatriating the hijacker in line with an agreement reached in 1990, but which was never signed.
Liu, 45, a jobless journalist, doused himself with gasoline and commandeered the airliner to China, complaining of political repression at home.
China returned the airliner, other passengers and crew on the same day, but took Liu into custody.
The Far East Air Transport jet, carrying 150 passengers and eight crew, was on a scheduled flight from Taiwan's southern city of Kaohsiung to Taipei when it was forced to China.
Taiwan had demanded Liu's repatriation, while Chinese officials debated whether to repatriate or prosecute him.
Taipei has offered to return two of the 16 Chinese who hijacked planes to the island.
Taiwan has banned air and shipping links with China for almost five decades, and insists such links must go through a third territory, mainly Hong Kong.
China called for reciprocity after agreeing to release Liu.
"We hope that the Taiwan side will take prompt measures to repatriate hijackers, in a bid to join hands in cracking down on hijacking," the association official said.

"We have consistently held that both sides of the Taiwan Strait should proceed from the overall interest in developing relations across the Taiwan Straits and protecting the safety of the lives and property of people across the Strait and cooperate in curbing the occurrence of hijacking," he said.
Taiwan has jailed 16 Chinese for hijacking 12 airliners to the island between April 1993 and June 1994.
Air piracy fell off sharply after Beijing launched a major drive to improve normally lax security at most airports.

The last hijacking of a Taiwanese airliner to China was in May 1986, when the pilot of a Boeing 747 cargo plane owned by Taiwan's flag carrier China Airlines commandeered the jet and flew it to Guangzhou.
The defecting pilot was hailed a hero and made a civil aviation official.
Beijing returned the plane and two crew members who did not want to stay in China after talks between the two rivals in Hong Kong.
